title: Diwali begins: Narakasura's dawn
hookLine: five days of light begin: a clean house, something new, and a demon defeated before dawn
carry: light defeats darkness, and the captives go free
last: SATSANG — THE COMPANY OF THE TRUE.

lines: A NEW POT, A SILVER COIN.
cards: A week before, it starts in the corners. Mothers and grandmothers pull everything off the shelves. Curtains washed, cupboards emptied, the dusty box under the bed finally dealt with.
Kids grumbling. Then the shopping: a new steel pot, a silver coin, new clothes. Then patterns of colored powder on the doorstep.
And finally the lamps, rows and rows of them on every windowsill and balcony, until the whole street glows. Now the practices become festivals. The biggest comes first.

teach.b: You know the name by now: a row of lamps, your deepa from day one hundred and twelve, multiplied by a whole country. What's new is the calendar.

Diwali falls in autumn, around the new moon, the darkest night of the month, usually in October or November. And for many families it's five days, not one; today, the first two. Different regions tell different stories.
You met the one many North Indians tell on day sixty-nine: Rama coming home to Ayodhya, and the city lighting lamps to guide him. Jains and Sikhs mark their own observances in the same season.
Day one is Dhanteras. Dhan means wealth, teras the thirteenth lunar day. The house has been cleaned, and now people buy something new, often metal: a pot, a spoon, a coin.
In the evening, many families set one lamp outside, facing south, for Yama, the lord of death, asking him to pass the house by. Day two is Naraka Chaturdashi, the fourteenth.
A demon king, Narakasura, had grown so cruel he'd imprisoned thousands.
Krishna, and in many tellings his queen Satyabhama beside him, defeated him and set the prisoners free. In much of South India and Maharashtra, this is the big morning.
People rise before dawn, rub their bodies with oil, bathe, put on new clothes, and the first firecrackers go off in the dark.

That's the teaching at Diwali's heart, the one every region's story shares: light defeats darkness, and good frees what evil locked away. Many teachers read it inward too: the lamp is knowledge, the dark is ignorance.
Clean house, clean body, and the darkest night is next.

how: In the days before Diwali, many Hindu families clean their homes thoroughly; on Dhanteras they buy something new, often a metal utensil or coin, and light a lamp for Yama in the evening; on Naraka Chaturdashi many, especially in South India and Maharashtra, rise before dawn for an oil bath and new clothes.

get up before dawn, oil bath, new clothes.
games.why: in much of South India and Maharashtra this is the big morning: people rise before dawn, bathe with oil, and dress in new clothes, remembering Krishna's victory over Narakasura and the prisoners set free.

practice: Find one small cluttered thing within reach, a drawer, a desk corner, your phone's home screen, and take one minute to clear it, the way families clean before Diwali.

Then, if you can, light a lamp or a candle, safely; if not, picture one on your front step, glowing outward into the dark street. If you pray, think of Krishna opening the prison doors; if not, just watch the light, and let it win.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. The festival of lamps, five days long: it begins with a clean house, something new, and a demon defeated before dawn. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhanatrayodaśī: dhana (wealth) + trayodaśī (the thirteenth lunar day). Dhanteras is the everyday Hindi form.

carryVoice: Your line: light defeats darkness, and the captives go free. The darkest night comes next. Day one hundred thirty-nine, done.
